instructions: Use package comments as the source of truth for package ownership boundaries. Flag changes that move GCE VM lifecycle, GKE cluster API reads, source node-pool selection, or provider policy into the wrong package. For pkg/metadata specifically, enforce that it remains a pure typed bootstrap metadata model and render boundary with no provider policy or API calls. For new user-visible behavior, consider whether an end-to-end test would cover meaningful GKE, GCP, or Kubernetes integration risk that unit tests cannot. Review changed hot paths and relevant dependency changes for concrete API amplification, lost cache reuse, and avoidable resource-scaled work; preserve freshness and ownership, and never present static findings as measured savings.

rules.rule: Provider changes should respect package ownership: instance owns GCE VM lifecycle, instance labels/tags, scheduling, capacity errors, zone operations, and provider-owned bootstrap policy; nodepooltemplate owns bootstrap source pool/template discovery; gke owns shared GKE cluster facts; pkg/metadata owns pure GKE bootstrap metadata modeling, parsing, typed mutation helpers, and Compute API rendering.

pkg/metadata must remain a pure transformation layer: no GCP API calls, no Kubernetes API calls, no source node-pool/template discovery, no GCE VM lifecycle decisions, no scheduler/capacity policy, and no in-place mutation of caller-owned Compute metadata templates.

Provider-owned bootstrap policy belongs outside pkg/metadata. Labels, taints, provisioning model, GPU behavior, disk compatibility, secondary boot disks, kubelet defaults, Spot shutdown behavior, NodeClass overlays, and source-template selection should be decided by provider packages and passed into pkg/metadata through typed helpers.

For new or materially changed GCENodeClass settings with a GKE equivalent, prefer GKE NodeConfig / Terraform google_container_node_pool.node_config naming, nesting, and semantics where practical, translating Terraform snake_case to Kubernetes camelCase. GCENodeClass spec already represents node configuration: do not add a nodeConfig wrapper. For example, use spec.advancedMachineFeatures.threadsPerCore rather than spec.threadsPerCore, spec.gvnic.enabled rather than a raw spec.networkConfig.nicType enum, and spec.minCpuPlatform for node_config.min_cpu_platform. Compare types, allowed values, units, defaults, and omitted versus explicit false/zero behavior; allow Kubernetes API conventions and documented differences required by Karpenter, GCE, or backward compatibility. Do not demand Terraform-only lifecycle behavior, unsupported GKE features, or renames of unchanged existing fields. Only flag a concrete avoidable mismatch, cite the equivalent GKE/Terraform field and reference, suggest the aligned shape, and account for any documented reason for divergence. Check that generated CRDs, docs, and examples agree with the chosen API.

New or renamed proposals must use a four-digit proposal number that has not already been used by another proposal. Check existing proposal filenames and proposal contents, including implemented or superseded proposals. If the new proposal explicitly declares its number in its contents, it must match the filename; references to other proposals do not declare the new proposal's number.

When a change adds or materially changes user-visible behavior that depends on real GKE, GCP, or Kubernetes integration, assess whether an end-to-end test would cover risk that unit tests cannot. Only flag practical, high-value scenarios that fit the existing test/suites infrastructure, such as provisioning, node registration or configuration, lifecycle, drift, consolidation, repair, networking, storage, or GPU behavior. Do not request end-to-end coverage for refactors, generated or documentation-only changes, or behavior already well covered below cloud and process boundaries. Explain the uncovered integration risk and suggest a compact test outline with the existing or proposed suite, setup, action, key observable assertions, and cleanup; avoid implementation-level detail.

For changed repeated paths, flag concrete client, RESTMapper, or cache recreation; unstable or incomplete cache keys; lost cache reuse; duplicate concurrent fetches that should be shared; and new uncached reads, N+1 API requests, or repeated discovery/pagination when cached state satisfies the same contract. Include dependency changes only when their affected call paths show such a regression. Preserve freshness, invalidation, credential rotation, and isolation between inputs; do not recommend caching every response. Cite the changed file and line, amplification mechanism and workload, and suggest a minimal fix or validation step. Do not invent measured savings or demand a bespoke benchmark or live E2E for every suggestion.

For changed controller/provider hot paths, flag concrete avoidable repeated decoding, full-list scans, large value copies, or repeated compilation of an unchanged regular expression in a loop or repeatedly called helper (including regexp.Compile, regexp.MustCompile, and package-level regexp.Match calls). Reuse compiled fixed patterns, but do not hoist input-dependent patterns or introduce an unbounded pattern cache. Preserve copies needed for ownership, safe mutation, and caller-visible behavior; do not request pointer/API changes solely because a value is large. Report only avoidable regressions introduced by the change, with the changed file and line, amplification mechanism, relevant workload, and a minimal fix or validation step. Static analysis is not a CPU, memory, latency, or monetary measurement; do not claim numerical savings without evidence or request a new test framework for every finding.
